text.en: Every day we use things like books, pencils and toys, and some of them help us work. Have you ever wondered how they work, and how they could work even better? Meera and Dhruv love finding out. On a Sunday they spin coins and cardboard spinners and watch them wobble or stand steady, and when rain falls they make paper boats and test what floats. Let us try the same experiments and find out together.

Meera spun a coin and watched it carefully, and you can spin things too. Objects like coins, bangles and wooden tops spin, but an eraser does not spin properly. As a coin slows down it begins to shake and finally falls, and a good scientist writes what she observes, what she wonders and what she thinks. Try spinning a coin, a bangle, a pencil, a piece of stone and a wooden top, and fill in what you observe and wonder.
Meera asked how a top spins, so they made spinners with cardboard pieces, toothpicks and the empty tube of a ballpoint pen. The textbook does not expect a complete scientific explanation; the aim is to play, try and give your own possible reasons. A spinner with the toothpick at the centre looks the same from all sides, so it stays upright and spins well. If the toothpick or the hole is away from the centre, the spinner may not spin properly, so the position matters. A square card looks circular when it spins fast, and you can try other shapes too. If a spinner fails, change one thing at a time, like the length of the toothpick or how it is lined up, to find what helps.
You can colour a spinner in different ways and see how the colours look when it spins. Many things around us spin, such as ceiling fans and the potter's wheel. A charkha, or spinning wheel, twists cotton fibre into thread, and Mahatma Gandhi used the charkha to make handmade clothes. Spinning tops have been used in India for thousands of years, and the lattu is a popular wooden top.
When the rain stopped, Dhruv and Meera made paper boats and put them in the puddle, and some floated properly while others flipped over. Take a leaf, an iron nail, an empty steel bowl, a stone, a plastic bottle with its lid on and aluminium foil, guess first, then drop them in water. Writing F for float and S for sink, you will find that a leaf floats and an iron nail sinks. Heavy things like iron nails sink and light things like leaves float, but this is not the whole story. Floating or sinking cannot be decided just by whether the object is heavy or light; other factors matter too.
Take aluminium foil and see what happens when its shape changes. When the foil is spread out, or made into a cup shape, it floats. When the foil is pressed tightly into a ball, it sinks. So by changing the shape we can make an object float or sink. Press the ball tightly so that little air is trapped, because a loosely pressed ball may even float.
In groups of three or four, think of how to make a boat from paper, cardboard boxes, ice-cream sticks, clay and adhesive tape. Draw a picture first, then make your boat, and try to make it different from the boats of other groups. Boats can be made from ice-cream sticks, coconut shells or walnut shells too. Compare boats in a class exhibition: some are strong and hard to break, some break easily, some tip over and some keep their balance. Think about how you can improve your boat, which is how designers work.
If something spins and slowly stops, like Ravi's spinner, you can ask why it slows down and what makes it stop. If a figure bends to one side, you can balance it by adding weight to the other side or moving the support. To classify objects, test them: wax, thermocol, a candle, a cork, a leaf and an ice cube usually float, while a marble, a coin and a spoon sink. Things like a tomato, an eraser or a lemon may depend on their kind, so test them and record what you see.

problem.en: A foil ball sinks but a foil cup floats. What does this show?

text.en: Both are made of the same foil with the same weight.
Only the shape changed.

why.en: The ball is small and compact, the cup is wide and holds air.

text.en: So shape can decide whether an object floats or sinks.

why.en: Floating is not only about heavy or light.

problem.en: Your spinner wobbles and falls. What can you change?

text.en: Check whether the toothpick is at the centre.

why.en: A toothpick away from the centre makes it unbalanced.

text.en: Change the length of the toothpick or the lining of the card.

why.en: Changing one thing at a time shows what helps.

text.en: Try again and record what happens.

prompt.en: Explain what you learnt about floating and sinking from the activities.

requiredIdeas.en: A leaf floats and an iron nail sinks
Heavy or light alone cannot decide it
The shape of an object can change floating or sinking, like aluminium foil

commonMisconceptions.en: All heavy things sink and all light things float

points.en: Spinners spin steadily when the toothpick is at the centre and the shape is balanced.
Things like fans, tops, charkhas and potter's wheels spin.
Floating or sinking is not decided only by heavy or light.
Changing the shape of aluminium foil can make it float or sink.
Guess, test, record and improve, as when making boats.
